Accordingly, Mr Chen’s unjustified dismissal personal grievance claim succeeded. What remedies should be awarded? Mitigation of loss Mr Chen appropriately mitigated his loss by obtaining new employment on 14 September 2023. Lost remuneration Section 128(2) of the Act requires the Authority to order an
operative_excerpt: that a penalty may be imposed for a breach of s 130(1) of the Act. Section 75(2)(e) of the HA03 provides that a maximum penalty of $10,000.00 may be imposed on a person who has breached s 81 of the HA03, by failing to keep holiday a leave records. Relevant law When assessing penalties the Authority is required to take into account the factors set out in s 133A of the Act. The Authority has also been guided by the Employment Court decisions in Borsboom (Labour Inspector) v Preet PVT Limited and Warrington Discount Tobacco Limited7 as summarised by the Employment Court in Nicholson v Ford8 and A Labour Inspector v Daleson Investment Limited.9 Objects of the Act Section 4B of the Act reflected the importance of an employer keeping legally compliant and accurate employment records relating to minimum entitlement provisions as being one of the three “key provisions” accompanying the Act’s objects. Section 4B of the Act required employers to keep records in sufficient detail to demonstrate compliance with minimum entitlement provisions, as defined in s 5 of the Act. Section 4B(2) of the Act provided that obligation was in addition to the requirements of any other provisions, such as ss 65 and 130 of the Act and s 81 of the HA03, relating to record keeping. One of the objects in s 3 of the Act is to recognise the need for trust and confidence and good faith behaviour in employment relationship and within the employment environment. Failure to keep employment records, so that an objective assessment can be made as to whether an employee has received their minimum entitlements, was inconsistent with good faith behaviour and fundamentally undermined the trust and confidence inherent in the employment relationship. Other objects set out in s 3 of the Act are to acknowledge and address the inherent inequality of power in employment relationships, and also to promote the effect of enforcement of employment standards.10 Nature of the breaches Mr Dai’s failure to keep any employment records for Mr Chen or to provide him with a written employment agreement involved ongoing breaches of employment standards that continued for the duration of his employment. The failure to pay Mr Chen 7 Borsboom v Preet PVT Ltd [2016] NZEmpC 143. 8 Nicholson v Ford [2018] ERNZ 393. 9 A Labour Inspector v Daleson Investments Ltd [2019] NZEmpC 12. 10 Section 3(a)(ii) and 3(ab) of the Act. his annual holiday pay is also an ongoing breach that has continued since 25 August 2023. Maximum potential penalty The maximum penalty for each breach by an individual such as Mr Dai is $10,000.00. Sections 62 and 130 of the Act and s 27 and 81 of the HA03 have been breached, so there are four ongoing breaches in total, meaning the maximum potential total penalty that could be imposed was $40,000.00. Globalisation Because two of the breaches that attracted penalties involved Mr Dai’s failure to keep employment records, even though those obligations occurred under different legislation, it was appropriate to reduce these two breaches into one globalised breach for the purposes of assessing penalties. Globalisation therefore reduced the four breaches to three breaches, which can be summarised as failures to keep employment records, provide a written employment agreement and to pay annual holiday pay when Mr Chen’s employment ended. That reduced the potential maximum penalty from $40,000 to $30,000. Were the breaches deliberate, negligent or inadvertent? The breaches were likely negligent. At the time the breaches occurred Mr Dai was the sole director of Construst, so he was personally aware it had obtained Accredited Employer Work Visa status. As such Mr Dai should have been aware of minimum code legislation, because Construst had been granted 20 work visa tokens by Immigration New Zealand around the time Mr Chen was employed by Mr Dai. Mr Dai had also run other businesses which had employed employees. He therefore ought to have known what his legal obligations were to Mr Chen regarding his employment. Mr Dai’s failure to meet his legal obligations as an employer was negligent. Impact of the breaches Mr Dai’s breaches of employment standards had a seriously adverse impact on Mr Chen, because his attempts to assert his legal rights resulted in Mr Dai deciding not to give Mr Chen any more work. It therefore resulted in Mr Chen’s unexpected unjustified dismissal, which had seriously adverse impact on Mr Chen, his family and their financial situation. Mitigation Mr Dai has not taken any steps to mitigate the adverse effects his breaches have had on Mr Chen. Previous penalties Mr Dai has previously had a penalty imposed on him for aiding and abetting breaches of employment standards in relation to another employee (Mr Jiao) who was employed by Construst.11 However, the Authority noted that the conduct in issue in this matter pre-dated the imposition of a penalty on Mr Dai in Jiao v Construst and Dai.12 This was therefore not a situation in which a penalty had been imposed on Mr Dai, who then subsequently repeated the same breaches. Culpability There is a high level of culpability. Mr Dai has run multiple businesses. He should have known what his legal obligations were. Even if he did not know, he could and should have obtained advice about that when Mr Chen raised concerns with him (Mr Dai). Consistency It is important that the penalty imposed in this matter was consistent with other cases involving similar breaches of employment standards. The Authority was satisfied that has occurred. Mr Dai’s ability to pay Mr Dai did not provide any evidence regarding his (in)ability to pay a penalty, so this is a neutral factor. 11 Jiao v Construst and Dai [2024] NZERA 530. 12 Jiao, above n11. Need for deterrence Penalties must be set at a level that will act as a deterrence to Mr Dai personally. Penalties also need to be sufficient to deter other employers more generally, who could be inclined to be lax regarding their compliance with employment standards and minimum code legislation. The level of penalty therefore has to send a strong signal to all employers throughout New Zealand that their business practices must uphold minimum code obligations, some of the most important of which is providing a written employment agreement, keeping accurate employment documentation and paying an employee correctly. Amount of penalties imposed on Mr Dai After considering all of these factors, Mr Dai is ordered to pay a total penalty of $2,750.00. This consisted of: (a) A globalised penalty of $1,000.00 on Mr Dai for breaching s 130 of the Act and s 81 of the HA03; (b) A penalty of $1,000 for breaching s 65 of the Act, being his failure to provide a written employment agreement; and (c) $750 for failing to pay Mr Chen his annual holiday pay when his employment ended. Proportionality It is important that the total penalty imposed was not disproportionate to the nature and extent of the breaches that Mr Dai is being punished for. The Authority was satisfied that overall the penalty imposed was proportional to the extent of the wrongdoing that has occurred. Should some of the penalty be paid to Mr Chen? Pursuant to s 136(2) of the Act, the Authority may order all or part of any penalty imposed to be paid to any person instead of, or as well as, the Crown. Mr Chen has been put to the time and expense of bringing these breaches to the Authority’s attention. It was therefore appropriate for Mr Dai to pay $1,500.00 of the total $2,750.00 penalty imposed to Mr Chen directly, to recognise the harm Mr Chen has personally suffered as a result of the breaches that occurred, for which he cannot be compensated. Was Mr Chen dismissed? A dismissal happens when the ending of the employment relationship occurs at the employer’s initiative. Mr Chen did not resign. He was ready willing and available to attend work, but could not do so because no work was given to hm to do. Mr Chen’s employment ended when Mr Dai decided not to give him any more work to do. Without work to do Mr Chen was not paid. Mr Dai’s advice to Mr Chen to go elsewhere if he wanted full time employment also indicated there had been a dismissal. Mr Chen was a permanent full time employee. Mr Dai was therefore obliged to provide him with work to do or if he was unable to provide work then Mr Dai still needed to pay Mr Chen who was ready willing and available to perform the work he had been employed to do. The failure of Mr Dai to assign Mr Chen any work to do effectively dismissed him. There was sufficient work to do, as was evident from the high number of recently employed employees from overseas who were working for Construst under AEWV work visas on the same construction site and projects Mr Chen was employed to work on. Alternatively, Mr Dai’s stance that PAYE was not going to be paid on Mr Chen’s wages and that Mr Chen was not going to be given a written employment agreement were fundamental breaches that made it reasonably foreseeable Mr Chen would not continue working in such circumstances. Mr Chen was therefore also able to establish he had been constructively dismissed, even if the failure to provide him with work had not amounted to an actual dismissal. Was dismissal justified? Justification is to be assessed in accordance with the justification test in s 103A of the Act. This required the Authority to objectively assess whether Mr Dai’s actions, and how he had acted, were what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time Mr Chen was dismissed.13 A fair and reasonable employer is expected to comply with its statutory and contractual obligations. Failure to do so could undermine its ability to justify its actions and/or dismissal of an employee. That was the case here. Mr Dai breached his statutory and good faith obligations to Mr Chen. Mr Dai reacted to Mr Chen’s attempts to obtain a written employment agreement by deciding not to give him any more work to do. That was a unilateral decision that Mr Dai made without consultation with Mr Chen. Mr Dai’s actions, and how he acted, was not what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances.14 He was therefore unable to justify Mr Chen’s dismissal. Accordingly, Mr Chen’s unjustified dismissal personal grievance claim succeeded. What remedies should be awarded? Mitigation of loss Mr Chen appropriately mitigated his loss by obtaining new employment on 14 September 2023. Lost remuneration Section 128(2) of the Act requires the Authority to order an employer to pay an employee the lesser of the sum equivalent to their lost remuneration or to three months’ ordinary time remuneration. Mr Chen was out of work for 19 days from 26 August to 13 September 2023. During the investigation meeting the parties calculated, and agreed, that if Mr Chen was held to be an employee, then his actual lost remuneration (based on the hours he had worked while employed by Mr Dai) was $5,236.53 gross. Accordingly, Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen actual lost remuneration of $5,236.53 gross under s 128(2) of the Act. 13 Section 103A(2) of the Act. 14 Above, n7. Distress compensation Mr Chen gave evidence about the stress, humiliation and distress his unjustified dismissal caused him. His family was put under “great financial pressure” which caused him to be “extremely anxious”, as he was reliant on his wages to be able to pay his mortgage. Mr Chen was very disappointed he lost his job. He told the Authority he suffered “significant psychological stress” as a result of his dismissal. Mr Chen described how his ability to eat and sleep was adversely affected and how it had caused him to lose confidence in himself and become depressed. Mr Chen said he felt deceived as he had lost his job for no reason. Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen $20,000.00 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act to compensate him for the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings his unjustified dismissal caused him. Should remedies be reduced to reflect contribution? Section 124 of the Act required the Authority to assess the extent to which, if any, the remedies Mr Chen has been awarded should be reduced to reflect any contribution he had to the situation that gave rise to his dismissal grievance. Contribution requires blameworthy conduct which has been proven on the balance of probabilities. Blameworthy conduct in this case was not established, so Mr Chen’s remedies were not to be reduced. Orders Within 28 days of the date of this determination, Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen $27,647.26 gross: (a) $760.00 wage arrears, consisting of unpaid annual holiday pay; (b) $80.00 unpaid petrol allowance arrears; (c) Interest of $70.73 on the amount of $840.00 (being the wage and petrol allowance arrears) that ran from 27 August 2023 (the date employment ended) to 17 January 2025, being the date of this determination; (d) $5,236.53 lost remuneration; (e) $20,000 distress compensation, without deduction (meaning this amount is tax free); (f) $1,500.00 partial penalty. Interest will continue to accrue on the amount of $910.73(consisting of the total wage and petrol allowance arrears of $840.00 plus $70.73, being interest to date) until that full amount plus all accrued ongoing interest has been paid to Mr Chen. All interest is calculated using the Civil Debt Calculator on the Ministry of Justice website. Within 28 days of the date of this determination Mr Dai is ordered to: (a) Pay a penalty of $1,250.00 directly to the Crown bank account; (b) Inform IRD that Mr Chen was employed by Mr Dai personally as an employee from 28 July 2023 to 27 August 2023; (c) Correctly calculate the PAYE and any other legally required deductions (such as ACC levy) that should have been made from Mr Chen’s earnings and remit those amounts in full to IRD under Mr Dai’s name as the employer against Mr Chen’s IRD number, as an employee. Mr Dai as Mr Chen’s employer is legally responsible for any penalties and/or interest IRD imposes due to Mr Chen’s tax on the wages he was paid from 28 July 2023 to 25 August 2023 not having been correctly paid by his employer. What costs should be awarded? Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, Mr Chen may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Mr Dai and Construst will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.15 Rachel Larmer Member of the Employment Relations Authority 15 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

case_name: IAN KEVIN RENNER v MANAWATU MOTORS 1970 LIMITED (t/a ROBERTSON MOTORS)
operative_excerpt: t commissions are owing. Did Mr Renner breach his duty of good faith owed to Roberton Motors? Mr Renner signed an employment agreement on 31 August 2020. There are three clauses contained in the IEA which are relevant to the claim Robertson Motors makes against Mr Renner. These are as follows: 30 Confidential information 30.9 During the course of employment or after termination of employment with the employer, the employee shall not directly or indirectly make a record of, or divulge, or communicate to any other person, any information regarding the employer’s business, or any matters associated with the employer. When requested, the employee hereby agrees to sign a Statutory Declaration stating that they are collecting commercially sensitive and valuable information only to perform the tasks required by the employer, that the commercially sensitive and valuable information will not be passed to others during and after the term of employment. The employee also irrevocably agrees to sign a Statutory Declaration stating they have returned all copies, in any and every form, of all commercially sensitive and valuable information on the termination of employment with the employer. 40. Non-solicitation 40.1 The employee shall not at any time during the period of employment or for a period of six months after termination of employment, for whatever reason, either on the employee’s own account or for any other person, firm, organisation or company, solicit, endeavour to entice away from or discourage from being employed by the employer, any other employee or actual client/customer or prospective client/customer of the employer. An employee who breaches this clause may be subject to disciplinary sanctions including possible termination of employment. 41. Restraint of trade 41.1 During the employee’s employment with the company the employee will be privy to sensitive and confidential information relating to the company’s business, and the employee may be in a position to develop and maintain relationships on behalf of the company with clients and other business associates. In order to protect the company’s interests the employee agrees that for a period of (3, 6, 9 or 12 months) after the termination of employment, the employee will not, either indirectly or directly: i. Own, establish, purchase, obtain an interest in, control, render services to, be employed by or otherwise be involved with or engaged by, whether for reward or otherwise, any business or enterprise which competes directly or indirectly with the business of the company, its subsidiaries, associates or affiliates, in the (state area or region restraint is to cover) region; ii. Solicit, canvass, entice or encourage any employee of the company to leave the company or interfere in any way with the relationship between the company and its employees; iii. Solicit, canvass, entice, deal with or encourage any client who is or was at any time during the last twelve (12) months of employment a client or customer of the company with a view to obtaining the business of that person/business; or iv. Interfere in any way with the relationship between the company and its clients, customers and employees. Robertson Motors say that Mr Renner breached one or more of the above provisions because, whilst he was still employed by them, he: (a) Solicited ShinMaywa away from the exclusive agreement it had with Robertson Motors; (b) Provided email contacts for ShinMaywa personnel to a client of the respondent; (c) Solicited or endeavoured to entice away clients/customers and/or potential clients/customers from Robertson Motors; (d) Did things to the detriment of Robertson Motors by promoting the relationships of its competitors, customers and clients with ShinMaywa rather than protecting and promoting the relationship of Robertson Motors with ShinMaywa. Robertson Motors also say that Mr Renner breached the non-solicitation provisions set out above because he has continued to solicit and entice away clients/customers and potential clients and customers. Mr Renner resigned in writing by letter, which although was dated 31 August 2023 was forwarded on 31 July 2023. The letter advised that his last day of employment would be 8 September 2023. Up until 8 September 2023, Mr Renner owed duties of good faith to Robertson Motors and was also bound by the provisions of his IEA both in relation to non-solicitation and restraint, and also his duty of fidelity and loyalty. Robertson Motors complains that during April 2023 and May 2023 Mr Renner used his work phone to communicate with a Mr Dudson of AB Equipment, a customer and potential competitor. Mr Dudson provided Mr Renner with his work email address. Robertson Motors says that this is evidence that Mr Renner was attempting to introduce AB Equipment to ShinMaywa. However, this evidence does not indicate that Mr Renner was acting against the interests of Robertson Motors. The employment agreement and duties of fidelity and loyalty do not prohibit Mr Renner from exploring other alternatives. What he cannot do is breach the specific provisions of his employment agreement or his implied duties of fidelity and loyalty and take any action to his advantage which may damage Robertson Motors. Robertson Motors takes issue with the fact that Mr Renner set up a company originally called New Life Beginnings Limited but latterly called Purpose Vehicle Solutions Limited. There is nothing in law which stops Mr Renner making arrangements for life post the end of his employment with Robertson Motors. The evidence was that Mr Renner’s company did not trade in any event and was originally set up so that an investment property could be transferred to it. The fact that this did not happen is by the by. On 13 April 2023, Mr Renner provided Mr Nishikawa and Mr Hiroki Takenaka of ShinMaywa with Mr Dudson’s email address. Whilst there is insufficient evidence suggesting a breach of the non-solicitation and/or restraint provisions of the employment agreement, it is difficult to see how providing ShinMaywa with Mr Dudson’s email address could be in the interests of Robertson Motors. The evidence shows that following this, a meeting took place between Mr Dudson and representatives of ShinMaywa. An email response states “Looking forward to new collaboration with AB Equipment”. Mr Renner did not discuss this issue with Robertson Motors and was certainly not acting in their interests. At this period of time, he was still an employee and was certainly not being active and constructive in maintaining a productive employment relationship. On 1 August 2023, Mr Renner emailed ShinMaywa advising of his resignation. This elicited a response back to Mr Renner “It may be necessary to think of a way how to continue and grow our sales activities”. The email to ShinMaywa was sent with no reference to Robertson Motors. A purpose of the notice period when an employee resigns, is to give an employer a chance to advise customers, suppliers and others of the resignation and take steps to protect their business. Advising Robertson Motors of his resignation on 31 July 2023, and then one day later sending an email to ShinMaywa unbeknownst to his employer may not on its own be a breach of non-solicitation or restraint provision, but nonetheless was certainly not helpful to Robertson Motors and could be seen as a breach of Mr Renner’s duty of good faith and fidelity and loyalty to his employer. At the very least he should have raised with Robertson Motors that was what he intended to as undoubtedly there would have been steps Robertson Motors would have wished to take. On 3 August 2023, Mr Renner emailed Robertson Motors largest customer, again forwarding email addresses for people at ShinMaywa. This was done without the knowledge of Robertson Motors. Again, this email was sent whilst Mr Renner was an employee owing duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty to Robertson Motors. It is difficult to see how he could have thought sending such an email was advancing the interests of Robertson Motors. ShinMaywa and Robertson Motors had a distribution rights agreement. The agreement gave Robertson Motors exclusive rights to sell listed ShinMaywa products in New Zealand. On 7 August 2023, a week after Mr Renner had forwarded his letter of resignation, ShinMaywa gave Robertson Motors notice that it was ending that agreement, meaning that Robertson Motors would no longer have the exclusive rights to sell ShinMaywa products in the New Zealand market. It is difficult to conclude other than if Mr Renner had not advised ShinMaywa of his resignation, that agreement would not have terminated at that time. By advising ShinMaywa one day after he had resigned but, during a notice period, Mr Renner deprived Robertson Motors from having a discussion with ShinMaywa regarding the effect of Mr Renner’s resignation. It is difficult to see that Mr Renner could possibly have thought his actions in communicating with ShinMaywa were advancing the interests of Robertson Motors. Indeed it is clear the opposite was true. Mr Renner’s actions constitute a breach of his duty of fidelity and loyalty which he owed to Robertson Motors. Mr Phil Arras, Chief Executive of NHR Group, gave evidence that he had known Mr Renner for some 20 years and that they were friends. An email from Mr Arras to ShinMaywa stated: Ian Renner gave me your email and asked me to contact you about how we may be able to help Ian set up the ShinMaywa business in New Zealand and navigate around his restraint of trade for three months. There may be a couple of ways to assist via the business I work at or through myself. Mr Renner accepts that he had a discussion with Mr Arras. Mr Renner also said that he did not believe there was any restriction on him setting up a business to compete with Robertson Motors. Whilst it is clear that that was a misguided view, equally, it seems that Mr Renner did not set up a business which competed. Nonetheless, having a friend contact ShinMaywa to instigate discussions for ongoing business, breaches Mr Renner’s duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty owed to Robertson Motors. In providing the information he did to third parties, Mr Renner breached the provisions of his employment agreement prohibiting him from removing or copying any confidential or commercially sensitive information. It certainly also breaches Mr Renner’s implied obligations of fidelity and loyalty to his employer. Restraint provision Mr Renner did not breach the restraint provisions contained in his employment agreement. He was not employed by any enterprise which competed directly or indirectly with Robertson Motors. There was no evidence he solicited, canvassed, enticed or encouraged any employee of the company to leave the company or interfered in any way with the relationships between the company and its employees. The evidence before the Authority made it clear that he did not solicit, canvass, entice, deal with or encourage any client of Robertson Motors to leave the business, with a view to obtaining the business of that person/business. Although there was some evidence that Mr Renner did want to continue a relationship with ShinMaywa, he said that that was in respect of ShinMaywa products that was not part of the prior exclusive agreement between ShinMaywa and Robertson Motors. Nonetheless, there is evidence that Mr Renner had some intention to breach the restraint provisions. He said he did not feel there was any obstacle to him owning and establishing a business in competition but as it transpires, although he took some steps in that regard, he did not breach the restraint provisions, although that may have been his intention. Summary of findings Robertson Motors did not unlawfully suspend Mr Renner. It did, however, breach its duty of good faith and acted in a misleading and deceptive manner in giving Mr Renner one reason for why it wished to take his laptop and phone when in fact it had another, namely a wish to forensically examine the devices seeking evidence of serious misconduct. Robertson Motors is required to pay commission on sales instigated by Mr Renner during his employment but which were completed after his employment ended. Mr Renner breached his duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty which he owed to Robertson Motors. He did this by dealing with ShinMaywa and others in a manner clearly designed to further his own interests and not that of Robertson Motors. This occurred during a time he was still an employee of Robertson Motors. Mr Renner did not breach the restraint provisions contained in his employment agreement. Orders In respect of the repossession of the laptop and phone, Robertson Motors breached the duty of good faith it owed to Mr Renner. It deliberately deceived him; however, Mr Renner also breached the duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty he owed to Robertson Motors. No loss was suffered by either party. Under these circumstances I decline to order a penalty against either party. Mr Renner is entitled to commission on sales he instigated prior to the termination of his employment but which were completed after his employment ended. The parties will need to work out and agree on what commission is due to Mr Renner. If the parties cannot reach agreement on this, then leave is reserved to return to the Authority which will hear evidence on quantum and issue a determination accordingly. Costs Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, either party may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.1 Geoff O’Sullivan Member of the Employment Relations Authority 1 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

case_name: ADO v JOAN FERNIE CHARITABLE TRUST BOARD
scope_support: were unjustifiably dismissed and unjustifiably disadvantaged. Acknowledging that reinstatement is the primary remedy, it is nonetheless the case that ADO is not without effective remedy should reinstatement not be ordered. In addition to awarding compensation for ADO’s personal grievance
operative_excerpt: In written submissions, counsel for ADO addressed the alleged disadvantage grievances on the basis that unjust baseless allegations were improperly raised. It was submitted that the grievance arose from allegations made in the course of correspondence in April 2024 from Mr Barham during a period of absence from the farm on the part of Mr Angland. [59] It is evident from the initiating email from Mr Barham on 16 April 2024, which referred to various performance concerns relating to tasks said to have been assigned to ADO by Mr Angland prior to his leave, that Mr Barham embarked on a course of making ill-advised allegations without due process. This included, without any meaningful investigation, statements that ADO had been dishonest and that there were ongoing competency issues. On 23 April 2023, Mr Barham then raised in a pejorative manner an allegation of sexually predatory conduct relating to the Complainant who was staying in another house on the farm. [60] Ultimately the issues raised by Mr Barham did not lead to disciplinary consequences. However, the actions in raising the allegations without any reasonable investigation or supporting basis were not actions that were open to a fair and reasonable employer in all of the circumstances. This was later compounded by Mr Barham sending correspondence to other individuals, including Mr McDonald, stating that ADO had lied about his historical responsibilities, advising them of allegations that ADO had been harassing a woman on the farm, and asking whether they had in their previous supervision of ADO “…had any issues of sexual predation/harassment of woman on Chesterhope…”. [61] The Complainant gave evidence before the Authority. In evidence, they accepted that ADO had made no sexually suggestive comments, that ADO did not touch or attempt to touch the Complainant, and that when ADO visited the house ADO knocked on the door and made no attempt to enter the house. Such as the Complainant had concerns, they boiled down to the Complainant’s perception that ADO knew they were home alone, and that ADO gave them a ‘filthy look’. The Complainant explained that they could recognise the behaviours as being predatory based on past experience. Mr Barham was informed of the concerns second hand. [62] The JFCT submitted that ADO was not disadvantaged in any way by the raising of the allegations or seeking of responses to its concerns. I disagree. I find that the allegations were raised in a vindictive manner, were improperly raised in an accusatory and conclusionary manner, and that the allegations were unjustifiably disseminated to other persons. The actions of the JFCT were also contrary to its good faith obligations and exposed ADO to ongoing unreasonable behaviour which was inconsistent with the requirement to be active and constructive in establishing and maintaining a productive employment relationship. [63] I find that ADO was unjustifiably disadvantaged in their employment by the JFCT’s putting the allegations to ADO in the absence of having a proper basis to do so. Such as ADO was unjustifiably disadvantaged by the making of unfounded allegations and the consequential actions of the JFCT, I find that the relevant actions relate to a single course of conduct, although separate from the dismissal itself, and remedies should be considered on that basis. What remedies should be awarded? Should ADO be reinstated on a permanent basis? [64] Section 125 of the Act requires the Authority to provide for reinstatement wherever practicable and reasonable.6 Reinstatement is the primary remedy. [65] ADO was unjustifiably dismissed and the dismissal was both substantively and procedurally unjustified. 6 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 125. [66] At present, the Stock Manager position remains vacant. There is conflicting evidence as to ADO’s suitability to perform that role. The JFCT’s position is that ADO could not perform the role and ADO maintains that they are able to perform that, or another suitable role. [67] There is evidence of significant disharmony between Mr Barham and ADO. ADO, when asked at the investigation meeting, could not positively affirm that they would be able to work with Mr Barham moving forward. [68] ADO says that they will lose income and be forced to vacate the farm accommodation. ADO also contends that they would be put into financial hardship, their funds would run out, and they would not have a home. ADO alluded to the difficulty they would have finding alternative employment, and in particular employment that comes with accommodation. [69] ADO maintains that they were willing to constructively engage in good faith if reinstated. They say that they can work constructively with Mr Angland and that interaction with Mr Barham is limited. ADO also contends that Mr Barham acted as a ‘lone wolf’. [70] The JFCT contends that there is no role for ADO to be reinstated to and that ADO remains unsuited to the Stock Manager position. [71] While I have found that the primary motivation in the JFCT’s actions related to conduct and performance concerns, albeit that I do not consider those concerns to have adequate justification, I also accept that there was some likely utility in the restructuring proposed. While it was not the primary basis for the dismissal, I consider that the organisational structure of the operations have changed, with those changes having solidified following the appointment of Mr Angland. Further, I find that, while the process followed was fundamentally flawed and that ADO may within a longer period of time have been sufficiently suited to carry out the role of Stock Manager, that the employment relationship has been dysfunctional for at least a part of the period of time during which the order for interim reinstatement has been in place. [72] Mr Angland says managing Chesterhope without a Stock Manager is challenging and that he has been undertaking additional duties at Chesterhope. He says undertaking those additional duties himself over a significant period is not sustainable, despite currently being assisted by casual shepherds with dogs. I accept his evidence. [73] I consider that reinstatement would have negative impacts, including on Mr Angland and the orderly and efficient operation of the business. I have no doubt that the working relationship, despite goodwill between the two and without suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of ADO or Mr Angland, has been strained by a combination of the relevant events. While those circumstances are very much attributable to the JFCT, I consider reinstatement in practical terms would be unsuccessful, problematic, and very likely would lead to further disputation. [74] ADO has been successful in relation to their claims that they were unjustifiably dismissed and unjustifiably disadvantaged. Acknowledging that reinstatement is the primary remedy, it is nonetheless the case that ADO is not without effective remedy should reinstatement not be ordered. In addition to awarding compensation for ADO’s personal grievances, the Authority’s investigation has found significant shortcomings and unfairness in the actions of the JFCT. [75] Having had the opportunity to hear further evidence as to the incident of 2 October 2023, while noting I am not satisfied ADO’s actions could be said to have contributed to the situation giving rise to their personal grievances, I find that the argument involved mutual disrespect and that in the context of the wider issues and developments since, that is relevant to the employment relationship now being dysfunctional. [76] I have considered the authorities referred to in submissions, including Maddigan v Director General of Conservation,7New Zealand Steel Limited v Haddad,8 and Genesys Telecommunications Laboratories Ltd v Scott.9 ADO’s submissions to the effect that the JFCT are the author of their own misfortune and that its actions should not be an impediment to reinstatement are not without some merit. However, on balance and having regard to the recently dysfunctional nature of the relationship, and having regard to the necessary relationships within an organisation with a very limited number of employees, I conclude that reinstatement would lead to inevitable problems that are likely incapable of being resolved. I also find that ADO would have significant 7 [2019] NZEmpC 190. 8 [2023] NZEmpC 57. 9 [2019] NZEmpC 113. difficulty working with or under the instruction of Mr Barham. I consider that an important fact notwithstanding that it would not be an everyday occurrence. [77] For the above reasons, and taking account of ADO’s responses at the investigation meeting regarding their employment and working with Mr Barham, I conclude that the employment relationship has irretrievably broken down and that reinstatement would be impracticable. I am not satisfied that it would be practicable and reasonable to order ADO be reinstated on a permanent basis. The application for reinstatement on a permanent basis is unsuccessful. [78] The order for interim reinstatement is rescinded and the parties should work constructively to make any necessary practical arrangements relating to the accommodation situation. In the absence of agreement being reached, ADO is to vacate the property within 28 days of this determination. [79] To the extent ADO provided an undertaking as to damages, I find ADO worked during the period of interim reinstatement and was otherwise willing to do so despite not being allocated tasks they were capable of performing. ADO’s conduct during that time was measured and reasonable and their actions in pursuing the proceedings, including reinstatement, were not without reasonable basis having regard to all of the circumstances. Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings [80] ADO has been profoundly impacted by the actions of the JFCT. Not only was the dismissal motivated by erroneous conduct and performance concerns, but there have been ongoing actions that have undermined ADO’s employment. Those actions have very clearly in my view amounted to unwarranted personal attacks. Additionally, the persistent allegations made against ADO, including from the time of the letter of 10 November 2023 containing allegations not relevant to the purported no fault redundancy process, have been demeaning and unwarranted. [81] ADO has also been subjected to ongoing unjustified criticism and demonisation. The impact on ADO has been compounded by the JFCT’s actions, including statements and allegations raised to the effect that ADO was a ‘sexual predator’, ‘lazy’, and ‘incompetent’. The dissemination of suggestions that ADO was a “sexual predator’ to other persons known to ADO are particularly egregious and the impact of that on ADO has understandably been profound. Not only were those matters not properly investigated, but they also unnecessarily inflamed the problems in the employment relationship and have impacted ADO on an ongoing basis. This has led to ADO experiencing shame and humiliation and I accept ADO’s evidence as to the impact in its entirety, including as to a loss of mana, self-confidence, and self-esteem. [82] I order that the JFCT make payment to ADO, within 28 days of this determination, of a total of $30,000 as compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings relating to their unjustified dismissal personal grievance. [83] I order that the JFCT make payment to ADO, within 28 days of this determination, of a total of $15,000 as compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings relating to their unjustified disadvantage personal grievance. Compensation for lost wages [84] ADO seeks compensation for lost wages, including for the period between the dismissal and interim reinstatement, that being 15 January 2024 to 4 March 2024. I consider that an appropriate approach is for ADO to be awarded a total of 7 weeks lost wages, totalling $8055.19, taking into account the period between dismissal and interim reinstatement. Contribution [85] I am required by s 124 of the Act to consider whether ADO’s actions have contributed to the situation that gave rise to the personal grievance. [86] Such as any performance and conduct issues have been raised, I do not consider that ADO’s conduct can be said to have been blameworthy in any meaningful sense. While relevant to the motivation of the JFCT, ADO’s conduct did not contribute to the circumstances giving raise to the personal grievance claims that have been made out. Having considered all of the evidence and submissions, I conclude that there is no relevant conduct on the part of ADO that contributed to the personal grievance and that the remedies to be awarded should not be subject to any reduction. Breach of good faith [87] The claim that the JFCT breached its good faith obligations relates primarily to an alleged failure to provide information relevant to the continuation of ADO’s employment and other actions said to have been designed to undermine the employment relationship. [88] I have otherwise concluded that the JFCT’s actions were not those of a fair and reasonable employer and additionally that those actions undermined the employment relationship. I consider that those matters have been adequately addressed by my findings in relation to the other claims and the remedies to be awarded. I decline to impose any penalty. Loss of monetary benefit – special damages [89] I am not satisfied that there is a proper basis on which damages or compensation should be awarded to reimburse ADO for the legal costs incurred relating to the restructuring process. [90] In terms of the costs that may have been incurred in relation to the employment process, those being incurred prior to, or independent of, the commencement of proceedings in the Authority, I am not satisfied that any such order should be made. Additionally, I am not satisfied that clear evidence has been presented identifying a “bright line” between ADO’s legal representation during the employment process and those incurred in relation to the Authority proceedings. Summary of orders [91] The order for interim reinstatement is rescinded. [92] The application for permanent reinstatement is declined. [93] The Joan Fernie Charitable Trust Board is ordered, within 28 days of the date of this determination, to make payment to ADO of a total sum of $45,000 as compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings relating to ADO’s unjustified dismissal and disadvantage claims. [94] The Joan Fernie Charitable Trust Board is ordered to make payment to ADO, within 28 days, of $8055.19 as reimbursement for lost wages. [95] ADO is to vacate the farm property within 28 days of this determination absent any other agreement as between the parties. Costs [96] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [97] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, ADO may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum the JFCT will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [98] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.10 Rowan Anderson Member of the Employment Relations Authority 10 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

case_name: ROBERT STOWERS v A B LIME LIMITED
scope_support: fair and reasonable employer could have concluded these three things as a result of the disciplinary process. Therefore, A B Lime’s dismissal was substantively justified. [42] Standing back from this and reflecting on what occurred the position was: (a) Mr Stowers had not attended work for almost five weeks and his inadequate communication during this time meant A B Lime had no clarity about why
operative_excerpt: Stowers in the afternoon as requested in that letter. In response to questions from counsel for A B Lime Mr Stowers accepted that he had consented to the proposed suspension but said he did so because he had no choice. (b) Mr Adendorff says there was no call on 10 May 2023 and he hand delivered the 11 May 2023 letter to Mr Stowers on the morning of 11 May 2023. There was a discussion in which Mr Adendorff outlined the points in the letter. There was no subsequent meeting on 11 May 2023 and no response from Mr Stowers regarding the proposed suspension other than that he stayed away from work, which A B Lime took as consent to the suspension. [20] In any event the position I have established, based on the evidence, is that: (a) Mr Stowers was suspended by A B Lime from 11 May 2023, and Mr Stowers accepted the suspension albeit because he believed he had no choice, and A B Lime assumed this consent based on the circumstances. (b) By 11 May 2023 Mr Stowers had received the two letters from A B Lime (3 and 11 May 2023) setting out its concerns over his absences from work and inviting him to attend a meeting on 15 May 2023. [21] On 15 May 2023 Mr Adendorff and Mr Stowers met. Mr Adendorff took handwritten notes in the meeting and then produced fuller typed notes shortly after the meeting. I have reviewed the notes and accept them as a contemporaneous record of the meeting. Based on these notes and the evidence of Mr Stowers and Mr Adendorff, I find that the key aspects of the 15 May meeting include: (a) Mr Adendorff explained that the purpose of the meeting was to go through the allegations as outlined in the letters so that he could hear Mr Stowers’ explanation and feedback. Mr Stowers advised he had received the letters and understood them. (b) Mr Adendorff reiterated (as set out in the letters) that the allegations were serious and disciplinary action up to and including summary dismissal was possible if proven. Mr Adendorff stressed that no decision had been made. (c) Mr Stowers explained that: i. He could not contact A B Lime whilst he was in custody. ii. Ms Adams had contacted A B Lime and told it that he was in custody, although he had not asked her to contact A B Lime. iii. He had regular contact with his father and an aunt whilst in custody but he did not ask them to contact A B Lime to explain his absence because he did not think of it. iv. He had contact with his lawyer but this was only after four weeks in custody. (d) Mr Stowers would not discuss why he was in custody or his pending charges but told Mr Adendorff could speak to his lawyer about this. (e) Mr Stowers accepted that there needed to be good communication with A B Lime. And he accepted that he had not contacted A B Lime whilst in custody, with his explanation being that he was in custody. (f) Mr Stowers understood that his actions could amount to a breach of his employment agreement. [22] On 17 May 2023 A B Lime provided its preliminary decision in a letter to Mr Stowers. In this letter A B Lime set out Mr Stowers’ explanations (as outlined in the notes) and then set out its preliminary findings – these were: (a) Mr Stowers had been absent from work without consent and had failed to take steps to advise A B Lime that he was in custody and unable to attend work. This behaviour constituted serious misconduct as set out in Mr Stowers employment agreement (clause 23.2(j)). (b) A B Lime needed to have trust and confidence in Mr Stowers acting in its best interests which included attending work as required in his employment agreement and making A B Lime aware as soon as possible if he could not attend. (c) A B Lime also had concerns about the pending criminal charges (having spoken to Mr Stowers’ lawyer) such that it had no certainty about the impacts on Mr Stowers and therefore A B Lime in terms of his work. (d) A B Lime no longer had trust and confidence in Mr Stowers to act with good judgement, attend work as required and when absent to notify A B Lime as required. [23] A B Lime’s preliminary decision, set out after its preliminary findings, was that dismissal without notice for serious misconduct was the appropriate outcome. [24] Mr Stowers was invited to provide feedback on the preliminary decision. [25] Mr Stowers provided feedback in a handwritten note. In this note he recorded that Ms Adams had advised A B Lime that he was in custody, whilst he was in custody he was unable to contact A B Lime and that he would like to keep his job. [26] On 23 May 2023 A B Lime recorded its final decision in a letter to Mr Stowers. After setting out his feedback it concluded that Mr Stowers failed to attend work without consent and this was serious misconduct. In terms of dismissal as a sanction for serious misconduct it stated that Mr Stowers’ employment agreement set out that serious misconduct may justify dismissal without notice, that it had no information from Mr Stowers about the pending charges and the impact on his ability to work, and that his failure to engage and respond has undermined A B Lime’s ability to have trust and confidence in him as a team member. In conclusion A B Lime’s final decision was that the serious misconduct and the irreparable breakdown in trust and confidence meant the appropriate disciplinary sanction was dismissal without notice. Suspension [27] Before I turn to consider whether Mr Stowers’ dismissal was justified or not I will briefly deal with the issue of Mr Stowers’ suspension. Whilst this was not raised in Mr Stowers’ personal grievance and it was not expressed in the statement of problem it became clear from Mr Stowers’ evidence and counsel’s submissions that he did not accept his suspension was justified. [28] In this regard, I accept that I can resolve an employment relationship problem essentially as I see it rather than being limited to how it is described by the parties.1 But in this employment relationship problem there are two impediments to concluding that the suspension was unjustified and awarding remedies as a result: (a) I do not have jurisdiction to resolve an unjustified action personal grievance, which would be the basis for an unjustified suspension problem, because a personal grievance of this type was not raised within 90 days. (b) In any event Mr Stowers’ accepted the suspension and A B Lime acted in reliance on that in suspending him – to deem A B Lime’s actions as unjustifiable in those circumstances would seem inappropriate. Issues for unjustified dismissal [29] So, this employment relationship problem is solely about unjustified dismissal. [30] If an employee has been dismissed the employer must prove that the dismissal was justified, in line with the test for justification and the duty of good faith set out in the Act.2 [31] The test for justification applies to two aspects of the dismissal: (a) The process by which the employer established what happened and whether dismissal should be the outcome. (b) The substantive rationale for the decisions made by the employer as to what happened and then the decision to dismiss. 1 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 160(3). 2 Employment Relations Act 2000, sections 4 and 103A. [32] Mr Stowers was dismissed by A B Lime; so, for this employment relationship problem, A B Lime must show that the dismissal was justified, both procedurally and substantively. The disciplinary process [33] In terms of process, in order to show that it has met the test for justification and good faith, A B Lime will need to show that: (a) It properly investigated what occurred in terms of the concerns it had about Mr Stowers. (b) It set out these concerns, provided relevant information and explained the possible implications of an adverse finding to Mr Stowers so that he could consider all of this and respond. (c) It gave Mr Stowers a reasonable opportunity to respond to its concerns, before it made its decision on what had occurred and whether this justified dismissal. (d) It properly considered the explanations given by Mr Stowers before it made its decision on dismissal. Substantive justification [34] Mr Stowers was dismissed because: (a) He failed to report to work without consent; this being serious misconduct. (b) His failure to communicate during his absence and his failure to engage over possible further absence given the pending criminal charges had undermined the trust and confidence A B Lime had in him. (c) For both serious misconduct and a loss of trust and confidence, dismissal without notice was appropriate. [35] In order to show that Mr Stowers’ dismissal was substantively justified A B Lime needs to establish that, on the basis of the process conducted, a fair and reasonable employer could have decided that Mr Stowers acted as it concluded, that is, that Mr Stowers’ actions amounted to serious misconduct and undermined trust and confidence and that dismissal without notice was appropriate.3 Analysis The disciplinary process [36] The disciplinary process conducted by A B Lime was sufficiently thorough and stepped through the requirements I have set out. Specifically: (a) A B Lime, through Mr Adendorff, investigated what occurred in terms of the concerns it had about Mr Stowers. The evidence is clear about what A B Lime understood about Mr Stowers not attending work and what it had been told (and therefore what A B Lime knew). AB Lime formulated its concerns based on an appropriate investigation. (b) A B Lime then set out these concerns clearly, in its correspondence of 3 and 11 May 2023. It was also clear in this correspondence that the actions if proven could be serious misconduct and this, in turn might justify dismissal without notice. (c) A B Lime did give Mr Stowers the appropriate opportunities to consider its concerns and respond, before it made its decision on what had occurred and whether this justified dismissal; Mr Stowers did consider all of this and respond both in the 15 May 2023 meeting and then his response to the initial proposal to dismiss. (d) A B Lime properly considered the explanations given by Mr Stowers before it made its decision on dismissal – this is clear from Mr Adendorff’s evidence and the correspondence. 3 Applying Employment Relations Act 2000, s 103A(2). [37] For completeness I record here that there has been no real complaint articulated by Stowers about the process. [38] Overall, I conclude that A B Lime’s process was what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances and was therefore justifiable. Substantive justification [39] It is clear that A B Lime had two issues with Mr Stowers’ conduct: (a) Mr Stowers had not reported to work and had not informed A B Lime of this, including why he could not attend. This spanned almost five weeks and whilst there had been contact from Ms Adams on two occasions this was inadequate as there was insufficient detail and clarity about what was happening. (b) It had no confidence that Mr Stowers would be able to continue to work because of the upcoming trial and there was no indication of possible outcomes and resultant impact on A B Lime regarding Mr Stowers’ ability to work. Further A B Lime had no confidence, based on the failure to engage by Mr Stowers, that he would communicate with it properly if he was unable to attend work in the future. [40] As a result of carrying out the disciplinary process A B Lime concluded that: (a) Mr Stowers failed to report to work without consent; this being serious misconduct pursuant to his employment agreement. (b) Mr Stowers’ failure to communicate during his absence and his failure to engage over possible further absences given the pending criminal charges had undermined the trust and confidence A B Lime had in him. (c) For both serious misconduct and a loss of trust and confidence, dismissal without notice was appropriate. [41] Reflecting on these conclusions by A B Lime I am satisfied that a fair and reasonable employer could have concluded these three things as a result of the disciplinary process. Therefore, A B Lime’s dismissal was substantively justified. [42] Standing back from this and reflecting on what occurred the position was: (a) Mr Stowers had not attended work for almost five weeks and his inadequate communication during this time meant A B Lime had no clarity about why he was absent and how long the absence would be. (b) A B Lime had no guarantees that Mr Stowers would be able to attend work in the future without further absence and, importantly, if further absences occurred it had no confidence that Mr Stowers would properly advise it of what was occurring. [43] In short, A B Lime had an employee who went missing for nearly five weeks without properly explaining why at the time and it had genuine concerns this could happen again if it continued to employ that employee. In the circumstances dismissal without notice was appropriate. Conclusion [44] A B Lime’s dismissal of Mr Stowers was justified. Summary [45] A B Lime’s dismissal of Mr Stowers was justified in the circumstances and this employment relationship problem is resolved in favour of A B Lime; no remedies are awarded to Mr Stowers. Costs [46] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [47] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, A B Lime may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Mr Stowers will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [48] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.4 Peter van Keulen Member of the Employment Relations Authority 4 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1
